items.title: Principles of diet (Ahara)
items.summary: Ayurveda treats food as the first medicine. What, how much, when, where and how one eats are all considered.

sections.h: Eight factors of diet (Ashta Ahara Vidhi Visheshayatana)

head: Factor
Meaning
rows: Natural qualities of the food (heavy, light, hot, cold)
Processing: cooking, soaking, roasting change its qualities
Place of origin and of eating
Time: of day, season, state of digestion
The person who eats: constitution, habit, digestive capacity

list: Eat warm, freshly prepared, slightly unctuous food
Eat the right quantity, after the previous meal is digested
Avoid incompatible combinations
Eat in a pleasant place, without hurry, without talking or laughing excessively
Eat attentively, considering what suits you

p: A classical guideline divides the stomach into thirds: one third solid food, one third liquid, one third left empty for digestion. In modern terms this is advice to stop before feeling full.

Classical principles fit well with balanced modern diets: plenty of vegetables, pulses and whole grains, limited ultra-processed food, sugar and salt. People with diabetes, kidney disease, coeliac disease, allergies or other medical conditions should follow their clinician's or dietitian's specific advice.

items.title: Shad Rasa
items.summary: Ayurveda classifies foods and medicines by six tastes. Each taste is formed from two elements and affects the doshas in a characteristic way.

head: Taste
Sanskrit
Elements
Effect on doshas
Examples
rows: Reduces Vata and Pitta; increases Kapha
Reduces Vata; increases Pitta and Kapha
Reduces Vata; increases Pitta and Kapha
Reduces Kapha; increases Vata and Pitta
Reduces Pitta and Kapha; increases Vata
Reduces Pitta and Kapha; increases Vata

p: A balanced meal includes all six tastes, weighted toward those that calm the person's predominant dosha. Excess of any one taste is said to cause disorders; for example, excess salt is linked classically to hair greying, wrinkles and bleeding disorders, which aligns with modern advice to limit salt.

items.title: Viruddha Ahara
items.summary: Charaka lists combinations and practices that are considered harmful even if each food is wholesome alone.

list: Milk with fish
Milk with sour fruits or salt
Honey heated or added to very hot food
Honey and ghee in equal quantities
Curd at night, or heated curd
Heavy food after a large meal (eating before digestion)

p: Charaka describes eighteen kinds, including incompatibility of place, time, digestive capacity, dose, habit, dosha, processing, potency, bowel state, health state, order of eating, rules of eating, palatability, combination, richness and the person's mental state.

Most of these rules have not been tested in clinical studies. Some align with modern advice (for example, avoiding very large or late meals). Do not avoid nutritious foods such as milk or fish altogether on these grounds alone, particularly for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Pathya Kalpana
items.summary: Light, easily digested preparations used during illness and recovery, especially after fasting or Panchakarma, in a graded sequence from thin gruel to normal meals.

head: Preparation
Description
rows: Clear liquid strained from rice cooked in much water
Thin rice gruel with a few grains
Gruel, often of rice or barley, sometimes cooked with herbs
Soup of pulses, especially green gram (mung)
Buttermilk: diluted, churned curd with the fat removed

p: After fasting or purification therapy, food is reintroduced gradually from Manda or Peya through Vilepi and Yusha to normal meals over several days, to let digestion recover. The exact sequence is set by the physician.

items.title: Simple healthy recipes
items.summary: Easily digested everyday dishes associated with Ayurvedic cooking. These are household recipes, not treatments.

list: Rinse ½ cup rice and ½ cup split yellow mung dal
Warm 1 tablespoon ghee; add ½ teaspoon cumin seeds, a pinch of asafoetida (hing) and 1 teaspoon grated ginger
Add rice, dal, ½ teaspoon turmeric and 4 cups water; add vegetables if wished
Simmer until soft (about 25–30 minutes, or 3 whistles in a pressure cooker); add salt to taste
Serve warm; finish with coriander leaves
Blend 1 part fresh plain curd (yoghurt) with 3–4 parts water
Add a pinch of roasted cumin powder, a little rock salt and grated ginger
Drink at room temperature with or after lunch
Avoid at night; avoid if you have a cold and congestion
Soak ½ cup whole green gram for 4–6 hours
Cook with 4 cups water until very soft
Temper with ghee, cumin, ginger and a pinch of black pepper
Add salt and a squeeze of lemon; serve thin

p: People with diabetes should be mindful of rice quantity; those with kidney disease should check salt and potassium advice with their doctor; dairy-free versions can use oil instead of ghee.
